note.specFocus: Why the Bible matters to Christians and why Christians interpret its authority differently.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
1.2 The Bible and Its Authority
The Bible is the foundational sacred text of Christianity, containing the Old Testament (shared with Judaism) and the New Testament, including the Gospels describing Jesus' life.
Why the Bible matters
• 2 Timothy 3:16 states "all Scripture is breathed out by God", meaning Christians see it as divinely inspired, not just a human historical document.
• The Gospels record Jesus' life, teaching, death and resurrection, giving Christians their central story and moral example.
• The Bible is used in worship, prayer, teaching and personal devotion, shaping both belief and daily conduct.
Different views of authority
• Biblical literalists/fundamentalists believe the Bible is inerrant (without error) and should be followed exactly as written, including, for some, a literal six-day creation.
• Liberal Christians see the Bible as written by inspired human authors within a particular historical and cultural context, meaning some passages are read symbolically or reinterpreted for today (e.g. many accept evolution alongside Genesis as a theological, not scientific, text).
• Catholics hold that Church tradition and teaching authority (the Magisterium) work alongside scripture in guiding belief; many Protestants hold to "sola scriptura" — scripture alone as the final authority.
Exam link: "Discuss whether the Bible should be read literally" answers should explicitly use the terms literalism, inerrancy and sola scriptura/Magisterium to show precise understanding.

questions.examTip: Make two separate points and develop each one. Link the development directly to the question.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. The Bible is believed to be inspired by God (2 Timothy 3:16, "all Scripture is breathed out by God"), so Christians treat it as a primary source of teaching about God's character and will for human life.

2. The Bible contains the Gospels, which record the life, teachings, death and resurrection of Jesus, giving Christians the central story and example that shapes their faith and moral conduct.
questions.question: Outline two reasons why the Bible is important for Christians.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Some Christians, often described as biblical literalists or fundamentalists, believe the Bible is the inerrant, literal word of God and should be followed exactly as written, including on matters such as the six-day creation.

Second, Other Christians take a more liberal approach, believing the Bible was written by human authors inspired by God within a particular historical and cultural context, so some passages should be understood symbolically or reinterpreted for the modern world rather than applied literally.

Finally, Denominational differences also affect authority: Catholic Christians hold that Church tradition and the teaching authority of the Magisterium work alongside scripture, while many Protestant Christians hold to "sola scriptura", the belief that the Bible alone is the ultimate authority for faith and practice.
questions.question: Explain why Christians have different views about the authority of the Bible.

questions.examTip: For a 10-mark discussion, analyse different aspects of the Christian issue and how they interrelate. Finish with a reasoned conclusion; do not just list advantages and disadvantages.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Literalists argue that because the Bible is the inspired word of God, it should be trusted and followed exactly as written; treating parts of it as merely symbolic risks undermining its authority and allowing people to pick and choose which teachings to accept.

A second consideration is: A literal approach to key texts, such as the resurrection accounts, is seen by some as essential, since if central historical claims are not literally true, the foundations of Christian faith would be seriously weakened.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Other Christians argue that parts of the Bible, such as parables told by Jesus or poetic sections like the Psalms, were never intended to be read as literal history, and that forcing a literal reading onto all of scripture misunderstands its different types of writing (genres).

A further consideration is: Taking some passages literally can also create tension with scientific understanding, such as evolution and the age of the universe, leading many mainstream Christians to adopt theistic evolution, reading Genesis as teaching that God created the world without requiring a literal six days.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: the answer often depends on which parts of the Bible are being discussed (history, law, poetry, parable), and whether a Christian's denomination emphasises scriptural inerrancy or interpretation guided by tradition and reason. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of inspiration, literal and contextual interpretation, Church teaching and applying scripture and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
